answer.rationale: Constraints eliminate the highest-confidence memory first: memory_b1 (rollback cleared the checkout error spike) is unusable because compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so its precedent value is zero here regardless of how well it worked on day 18. memory_b2 (regional failover) is the most dangerous fit: it was validated on a latency degradation, and the archived summary says 'traffic shifted cleanly' — it says nothing about in-flight write durability, and we are at settlement peak with heavy writes. Failing over mid-peak is precisely the scenario where 'restored latency fast' could coexist with lost customer writes, which violates the primary objective. memory_b4 (circuit breaker) contained an external partner dependency outage; our symptom is internal write-path contention with no named failing dependency, so failing fast would shed exactly the settlement writes we must not lose. That leaves memory_b5 and memory_b3. memory_b5 is the closest mechanistic match: read load on the primary was displaced and transactional write latency recovered same-day — same organ, same failure mode. memory_b3 is the plausible alternative but its evidence is a *pre*-provisioned headroom buffer ahead of a known peak, measured on queue depth during a promotional (likely read-skewed) surge; it is not evidence that capacity added 90 minutes into an active write-path incident will land in time, and capacity provisioning has the longest lead time of any option. So I verify b5 (the memory I intend to act on) and b3 (the memory that would change my mind), and leave the eliminated ones unverified since verification cannot unblock them. Important caveat on the memory set as a whole: all six records are success stories, consolidated summaries with sources archived. That is a survivorship-shaped corpus — it tells me what worked and is silent on what was tried and failed, so my prior on any single tactic is inflated. I want the b5 source record specifically to check whether the day-55 incident was also under peak write load or during a quiet window, and whether replica lag was bounded. Acting at small_guarded_test scale rather than broad: shift a bounded slice of report/dashboard queries off the primary first, watch p99 and replica lag together, and expand only if write latency actually bends. This is reversible within minutes and loses no writes, which is the property the other four options lack.
